query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the high‐temperature single-phase BCC structure is metastable because the alloy’s intrinsic thermodynamic driving force—primarily the strong negative mixing enthalpies between Al and Ni (and also with Co)—favors the development of short-range order and eventual B2-type ordering. However, the diffusion‐slowed kinetics in this multicomponent system delay the ordering transformation. Therefore, only when sufficient thermal exposure (or slow cooling) provides enough time to overcome the kinetic barriers will the alloy transform from the high-temperature disordered BCC state into a mixed state with emergent ordered (B2) regions and a compositionally partitioned disordered BCC phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature single-phase BCC (disordered solid solution) state
generation.intervention: Thermal treatment with controlled cooling rates (comparing rapid quenching versus slow cooling/annealing)
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted within the temperature range from near melting down to below the predicted ordering onset temperature (approximately 1600 °C) with varied residence times; ambient pressure; same nominal composition
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering driven by strong Al–Ni (and Al–Co) pair interactions leading to the formation of B2-type nano-domains
generation.mechanism: A competition exists between the thermodynamic instability of the disordered BCC phase (with a free-energy reduction upon developing short-range order and eventual B2 ordering) and the kinetic hindrance caused by sluggish atomic diffusion in a multicomponent alloy. Under slow cooling, atoms have sufficient time to rearrange locally, enabling phase separation into an ordered (B2) phase (enriched in Al, Ni, and Co) and a remaining disordered BCC phase (enriched in Cr and Fe). Rapid cooling suppresses this ordering despite the thermodynamic drive.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to slow cooling or prolonged annealing will exhibit measurable signatures of ordering (such as emerging B2 superlattice reflections and compositional partitioning between an ordered domain and residual BCC matrix), whereas rapidly quenched samples will retain the high-temperature disordered BCC microstructure. The extent of ordering and phase separation should correlate with the thermal exposure time and the degree of undercooling relative to the ordering onset temperature.
generation.baseline: The disordered high-temperature BCC state obtainable by rapid quenching serves as the baseline, whereas any deviation (i.e., appearance of B2 ordering and compositional segregation) upon extended thermal treatment indicates the influence of the thermodynamic drive acting over kinetic timescales.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid for Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys near the specified composition and within the thermal regime where the ordering driving force becomes significant (roughly below ~1600 °C) but before complete equilibrium is reached. Extreme deviations (e.g., very rapid quenching or non-isothermal processing with negligible residence times in the ordering temperature window) may preclude the appearance of ordered domains.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature at which the ordering onset becomes dominant and the quantitative extent of the free energy difference between the disordered BCC and ordered B2 phases remain to be determined experimentally. Additionally, potential effects of minor fluctuations in local composition and processing inhomogeneities might influence the ordering kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples and subject them to identical thermal histories except for the cooling rate. One set should be rapidly quenched from the high-temperature BCC state, and another set should be slowly cooled or isothermally held in the temperature window below ~1600 °C. Examine the microstructures with techniques sensitive to ordering (X-ray diffraction for superlattice peaks, TEM for ordered domain identification, and compositional mapping via EDS).
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns (appearance or absence of B2 superlattice reflections)
Transmission electron microscopy imaging of grain interiors for nanometer-scale ordering
EDS compositional mapping to detect partitioning of Al, Ni, and Co versus Cr and Fe
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to observe exothermic/endothermic peaks corresponding to ordering transformations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowly cooled/annealed samples do not exhibit any evidence of B2 or other ordering (i.e., if they remain indistinguishable from rapidly quenched BCC microstructures) despite sufficient residence time in the predicted temperature window, or if ordering appears irrespective of the cooling rate, then the hypothesis that the interplay of thermodynamic ordering drives phase transformation (modulated by kinetic barriers) would be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Kinetic effect and tailoring phases in CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA
cited_evidence.text: Our results indicated that kinetics of phase transformation plays a crucial role in phase selection of the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA. The phases can be controlled using kinetic ways according to the CCT curve. It seems that the sluggish diffusion in HEAs did not affect the kinetic behavior in this alloy system especially in the intermediate temperature. In fact, kinetic effect not only works for the special CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA but affects the phase selection of all HEAs. Li et al. reported that BCC phase can be obtained by supercooling method in the well-known FCC single phase CoCrFeNi HEA and the mechanical properties of the HEA was enhanced by three times. The rapid solidification behavior of CoCrCuNiFex HEA was also studied and useful nano-phases were found in the matrix, which would unquestionably strengthen the HEA dramatically. Ravi et al. reported that synthesis route can have a significant influence on the process of phase-choice and -evolution in different HEAs and this is actually a result of kinetic effect. cited_evidence.kind: web:Temperature-dependent ordering within the BCC solid solution
cited_evidence.text: We observe the following trends for AlxCoCrFeNi, for the range 1 < x < 2, summarized in Fig. 7: there is a strongly x-dependent B2-ordering temperature, ranging in the simulations from approximately 1220 °C for x = 1 to 1850 °C for x = 2. For x = 1, this value is close to the temperature where B2 superlattice peaks are first observed (Fig. 4b). These compounds melt near 1300 °C (Fig. 4a, b). Thus, for x = 2, the prediction is that the compound will have strong B2 order on solidification, consistent with our scattering experiments (Fig. 4a). We predict that the system will have weak B2 order on solidification for most compositions in this range. We further predict a weakly x-dependent temperature where the B2 and BCC solid solutions become strongly separated. This unexpectedly sharp transformation occurs very closely to an observed change in the microstructure, using in situ microscopy during heating (Fig. 6b, c), and at a temperature very close to a peak observed through calorimetry for x = 1 (Supplementary Figure S3).
